It was not my fault. A friend of mine parked very close to my silver 2024 Suzuki in the parking lot. He accidentally scraped my car while maneuvering. It wasn't even my fault. The car was scraping my side while trying to back out. He didn't see my signal lights and drove right into it. I'm not hurt, but we're going to need some estimates on the damage. The car scrape isn't really visible, so it'll cost around 9800-12200 shekels.

Thursday mid-morning, May — late spring (dry) I was driving home from work, entering the residential section of Petah Tikva. A black 2022 Volkswagen, following closely behind, abruptly reversed without signaling, colliding with the back of my car. The collision damaged my windshield glass and the dashboard, leaving a shallow dent near the engine compartment. The other car sustained some scratches on its roof panel. We exchanged contact information briefly before leaving each other alone. It was my fault. I'm taking responsibility for the damage. The minor repair costs are estimated between 2,200 and 3,300 shekels.

Wednesday evening rush hour, March. It was cloudy, no rainfall, calm streets. I was parked outside a supermarket near Herzl Square when a white Mini suddenly pulled backward into me, hitting my passenger side door. I swerved sharply to avoid it, but the force knocked me out of control onto the sidewalk. A few minutes later, emergency services arrived and helped me off my car. The Mini owner admitted liability immediately and offered compensation within the specified limits. They agreed I would receive 4000 shekels under Israeli regulations for property damage and personal injury protection. The police also took photos and statements from everyone involved. My car sustained moderate scratches along its side, similar to a shallow scrape done by an errant golf ball. No one was seriously hurt, though our interactions ended abruptly due to the sudden loss of balance from the collision. I am very relieved everything turned out fine, even though the incident left me shaken. My primary concern now is making sure my finances remain intact until receiving the settlement money.

It was not my fault. Another driver scraped my car while maneuvering in the parking lot and admitted it. The rear bumper was dented moderately, approximately 12,000 shekels worth of damage. It was Tuesday mid-morning, October, raining. My car is a white 2020 Toyota parked in the same lot as the incident.

Tuesday evening, rainy season started, night clear. I changed lanes without noticing the car already beside me and scraped its side. It was my fault, taking responsibility now. The damage is approximately 1500 shekels. The road was wet, making slipping more likely. This incident occurred on the Haifa highway, near sunset.

I was driving down Ashdod Highway when suddenly, several vehicles swerved out of control into the middle lane, colliding head-on into each other. It was pitch black outside, but the sound of screeching tires filled my ears. I couldn’t find any signs of who could possibly be at fault, so I kept my eyes peeled for anyone who might’ve been involved. By the second sentence, I knew it was impossible to determine who caused the accident. There were no witnesses around, and no camera footage captured the entire event. The damage assessment came back as severe: approximately 30,900-46,400 shekels worth of dents, scratches, and damages. My 2017 Volkswagen had taken quite a battering from the chaos unfolding around me.

Sunday afternoon in Petah Tikva, late spring in mid-morning sunlight, clear skies and a crisp breeze blowing. I was tailgating the car in front of me on the narrow, two-lane road when suddenly, without warning, it braked sharply, causing my vehicle to veer off course. My car reversed several feet backward, colliding with the bumper of the vehicle directly ahead. It was my fault. The collision was severe, approximately 14,700-22,000 shekels worth of damage. The exact amount isn't precise, as the damage is extensive—multiple dents, scratches, and some bodywork involved. The police report shows signs of extreme force and rapid braking from both vehicles, confirming our mutual recklessness.

I was driving slowly down the quiet residential street during the peaceful dawn hours of Wednesday. My focus was solely on maintaining my safe distance from the bicycles and pedestrians on either side. Just before reaching the crosswalk, I noticed an unusual sight—another car inching through the pedestrian zone without any intention to yield its right-of-way. The moment I realized what was happening, I applied gentle braking to avoid a collision, but the car in front continued forward at a dangerous pace. Despite the warning signs, I couldn't believe the other driver wasn't paying attention. By the time I reached the crosswalk, the car in front had swerved off onto the sidewalk and then darted into the nearby driveway. It seemed almost negligent, as if the driver hadn't even noticed my presence until it was too late. It was NOT my fault. The other driver hit me, causing severe damage to my car—a moderate dent in the bumper and some scratches on the interior dashboard. The cost will range from approximately 12,900 to 19,400 shekels.

I was parked at a local café on Friday afternoon in February, waiting for a friend when I heard the distant rumble of an engine. A blue 2022 Ford suddenly reversed backward into my vehicle, blocking my door with its bumper. I tried to move the car out of harm's way, pushing against the back doors to try and clear a path, but nothing worked. The other driver’s car was several meters behind, making it easy for him to see that I wasn't responding quickly enough. When I finally emerged, blood trickled down the side of my car. It was not my fault, the other driver hit me.

Thursday evening rush hour, August, Bat Yam. It was cloudy with no rain. My 2013 Nissan was parked near an empty lot. When I returned, the windshield wipers rattled against the outside mirror frame. There was nothing written in the passenger seat, no cameras around. I couldn't see any witnesses, so it’s hard to say who broke my window. The damage assessment: about 7000 shekels. The crash happened when I tried to reverse out of a tight space in the middle of the night. The other car, which I didn’t see clearly until it was almost here, went straight past without signaling. Despite honking repeatedly, it kept heading straight, leaving me no room to avoid hitting its bumper, even though I was backing up slowly. After we collided, the taxi driver sped away before police arrived. I’m lucky I didn’t get more than a few scratches, but the glass shattered badly inside my car. I’ve got quite a few scratches now!

On a Tuesday during the evening rush hour in May, while driving on an empty stretch of the highway near Bnei Brak, I was attempting to merge onto the next lane without signaling when I suddenly felt the ground shake beneath my wheels. My blue 2023 Suzuki began swerving wildly, its bumper slamming into the back of a slower-moving vehicle ahead of mine, causing both our cars to slide sideways and collide head-on. When I finally regained control, the damage was evident—the vehicle to my right lay twisted and dented, its rear end crushed against my front windshield. Despite being driven under heavy traffic conditions, the incident left an estimated damage cost of 41,200-49,720 shekels, clearly attributing fault to the other driver who lost control due to distraction.

The day started hot and dry with a clear sky. It was mid-morning rush hour in Kfar Saba. Wednesday’s heat made the streets more congested than usual. Cars zipped past me at high speeds, swerving to avoid the throngs. Around 8 AM, I approached an intersection marked by a green light. My eyes adjusted quickly, but before reaching it, I noticed a small delay ahead—another car blocking the lane. Suddenly, from out of nowhere, a sleek silver sedan roared through the gap, its tires screeching on the wet asphalt. Its wheels spun wildly, creating sparks. A cloud of dust kicked up as I braced myself, waiting for the worst. But the collision felt slow and distant. When it finally happened, I realized the other driver had overstepped the mark, slamming into my car from behind like a boxer hitting another. My Peugeot’s rear bumper smacked solidly into the back window of the passing car, sending shivers down my spine. By the time the emergency services arrived, our vehicles were a mess—a perfect example of a rear-end collision.

I entered an intersection when I didn’t have the right of way and hit the side of a crossing car. It was my fault, and I take responsibility. My car’s bumper is severely dented, with the dent extending about 4 inches from the edge of the hood. The total damage comes to approximately 17,000 shekels.

I was parked on a busy sidewalk near the bus station in Petah Tikva when suddenly, a van swerved out from an intersection and struck my green 2017 Suzuki directly in front. Visibility was poor due to heavy fog, making it difficult to spot any movements. The van's driver seemed distracted and appeared unbothered by the collision. The van skidded to a halt beside my car, its side facing forward striking mine. The impact wasn't strong enough to cause extensive damage immediately, but it clearly dislodged some of the rearview mirrors. There was a noticeable dent in the passenger-side door frame. By the second sentence, I stated plainly that it was unclear who was responsible—no one saw the incident, and there were no witnesses or cameras available for verification. Despite the lack of clear evidence, I mentioned the approximate damage in shekels: about 7,900-11,800. Physically, I reversed backward, taking a few steps back before attempting to move my car further away from the scene.

It was 7 AM on a bright Monday morning, May. My silver 2022 Honda was parked neatly on Binyamina Street in Netanya. The air was crisp, the sky clear blue, and the ground underfoot hard-packed asphalt. Around 7:30 AM, a silver BMW skidded past my bumper. It was barely noticeable at first—just a small scrape against the rear window—but then something strange happened. A few moments later, the BMW slid forward, sending its rear end inches away from my windshield. It wasn't my fault. That BMW struck me, leaving behind what felt more like scratches than damage. When I tried to pull over, the scuffs turned to cracks, tiny lines showing where the wheels touched my car. The damage estimate came to about 2900 shekels. Minor, yet unsettling. And yes, I'm aware that I'm not the cause here. It was the other driver who caused all the trouble.

Friday evening rush hour, morning of March. It started clearing up around midnight, so the sky was still bright but almost devoid of clouds. I was driving home from work when I noticed something strange—my white 2022 Ford was stuck in a pile of cars, all facing the same way, like a scene out of a horror movie. As soon as I came to a complete stop, another car slammed into the back of mine, pushing everything forward. I couldn't believe what was happening—I wasn't even in control! The other driver didn't seem to notice anything wrong until we bumped together, leaving our vehicles dented and totaled. The collision happened on Modiin Highway, near the exit ramp towards town. The street was relatively clear, just a few parked trucks and delivery vans scattered about. Visibility was good; no fog, no precipitation. I could see clearly ahead of me, though now it seemed like I was running blind due to the sudden shift in momentum. When I finally stopped, the damage looked pretty severe. My car wasn't completely totaled yet, but every panel was scraped and dented.

Friday morning rush hour, around 8 AM, Tel Aviv, raining moderately. Wet roads posed an extra challenge. I was driving slowly through a crowded pedestrian zone, judging the distance carefully due to heavy foot traffic. Unfortunately, I misjudged the space, bumping into another vehicle from behind. It was my fault. The rear-end collision caused significant damage — approximately 6400-9600 shekels worth of repairs. The police were called, and the incident was recorded. My silver 2011 Kia sustained substantial damage. The rainy weather conditions exacerbated the situation, affecting visibility further.

On a Friday around midday in October, my car was struck while stopped near Ramat Gan. Wet roads had delayed visibility, making it hard to spot another car backing out without looking. It was not my fault; the reverse driver caused the accident by hitting my vehicle from behind. The damage assessment came to roughly 12,000 shekels. I took photos immediately, hoping to provide clear evidence for any claims process.

I was backing out of my driveway early in the afternoon, trying to avoid the traffic jam building up around me. When I turned onto the main road, I saw my neighbor's garage ahead and hesitated. Just as I started to back out, a truck veered into my lane and hit the fender of my parked car. There was barely any dent, just a slight scratch. I realized I should have been paying closer attention! My car looked fine, and the scratches weren't major. It wasn't a total disaster. I took some pictures to prove it. It was definitely my fault, so now I need to find my neighbor's contact info and explain everything clearly before filing a claim.

Wednesday in the afternoon, November in Netanya, I was involved in a reversing collision with my black 2023 Hyundai. We were both at fault and share the blame. The estimated damage to my car is ₪3200-4800.

I was driving slowly through a crowded pedestrian zone, trying to avoid running over an elderly man crossing ahead of me. In my haste, I misjudged the space between the pedestrians and the building's barrier, causing my car to collide with another vehicle from behind. It was my fault, and the damage was minimal—roughly 1600-2400 shekels worth. It was my fault. A collision with a car from behind. The damage wasn't severe—it amounted to about 1600-2400 shekels. The city was bustling with people, so visibility was poor. The summer heat kept the streets hot, but it was clear outside. My silver 2023 Toyota, slightly dented, came to a halt in the middle of the sidewalk.

Tuesday around midday, July. Bat Yam. Clear skies, hot and dry conditions. It was not my fault. A white 2024 Ford inched through the pedestrian zone, causing my car to collide with its back end. Witnesses reported seeing the other driver speeding through a yellow light. Despite braking hard, I failed to avoid the collision. The damage is minor, approximately 3100-4600 shekels. Both vehicles sustained superficial scratches and dents. The incident occurred due to poor judgment in merging into traffic at high speeds.

While reversing out of the driveway, I hit a car parked behind me. It was pitch-black outside, and I couldn't see anything until I backed up completely. My 2016 Seat bumped its bumper, damaging the windshield and the roof slightly. I tried calling emergency services, but got no response. When I finally reached the owner later that day, we exchanged contact information reluctantly. The damage checks came back about $1500. That night, the police didn't even bother coming.

Wednesday night, late autumn in Ramat Gan under clear skies, temperatures dropping gently. My 2023 Nissan lay silently, a shadow cast over its polished exterior. It wasn't my fault—the other driver, a swift reversal backward, sent my car tumbling back, leaving a trail of rusted metal and shattered glass behind. A heavy sigh escaped me before the lights flickered off, plunging the quiet night further into darkness.

Friday afternoon, 2:30 PM, in Netanya. I was stopped at an intersection, looking for a spot to park under the hot summer sun. Another driver, reversing backward, struck my car from behind. The crash pushed my car back about half a meter. No one was seriously hurt, but both our vehicles sustained minor damages - approximately 3,600 shekels total.

Driving slowly down Ramat Gan Street, I noticed an unexpected lane divider ahead blocking my path. Without checking, I braked hard but missed it, entering the wrong lane. Behind me, a sleek black BMW zipped past too quickly, leaving no room for maneuvering. My bumper collided with the BMW's rear bumper. It was a momentary clash, like two trains bumping at a station platform without warning. I swerved sharply to avoid another collision, nearly hitting a parked truck in the next lane. A few seconds later, traffic eased back up, but now all eyes were on our encounter. Cars honked, pedestrians stared. Yet none moved closer, unsure who to blame. The collision caused a scratch on my side mirror, some paint chips from the chrome grille. The windshield wipers squealed as I tried to clear the small stain. Despite minimal visible harm, the impact rattled my nerves. The damage assessment suggested around 2000 shekels for repairs. It was my fault, plain and simple. The BMW’s sudden approach could be seen from a distance.

It was a sweltering Thursday evening in August in Ramat Gan, hot and clear night skies provided little relief from the oppressive heat. My 2024 Volkswagen, a pristine white beast, was idling at a traffic signal at the start of our journey home. Just before we merged onto the highway, our paths crossed unexpectedly. We were both heading towards the same lane, attempting to merge at the same split second. I was trying to go straight ahead, but without noticing her hesitation. She was turning right, unaware of the chaos around us. As I attempted to pull forward, our vehicles collided, sending shivers up my spine. Both of us braced ourselves, ready for the worst. But miraculously, nothing serious happened. The impact was mild enough that neither of our bodies felt any pain immediately afterward. Just some minor scratches here and there. When I got out of the car, the air conditioning kicked back on, but I couldn't shake off the lingering heat. The repair bill came out to about 7000 shekels—just under half a tonne for such an incident.

Sunday morning rush hour started early in Tel Aviv. Clear skies greeted the commuters as they headed towards their destinations. I, a white 2023 Kia, was about to begin my commute home. As I approached the intersection, I noticed another driver ahead of me signaling to turn left. Following closely behind, we all swerved into the same lane, increasing our chances of getting caught up in the traffic flow. However, none of us paid close enough attention to the surrounding vehicles. Suddenly, a loud crash echoed through the air. My car screeched to a halt, and I looked back to see what had happened. A taxi, traveling in the opposite direction, had slammed into mine. Both our vehicles were damaged, though neither sustained significant injuries. The taxi driver was traveling much faster than the rules allowed, which was the cause of the accident. Neither of us could justify our actions in hindsight—our negligence led to this unfortunate event. The taxi driver was heading straight toward me, trying to avoid the intersection. In the chaos, I couldn't see him clearly until it was too late.

Sunday evening rush hour. Clear skies over bustling Jerusalem streets. My 2024 gray Mazda approached an intersection with two oncoming traffic streams, inching closer than necessary before I realized the danger. We shared the blame for our collision, both vehicles scraping and dented. The total repair cost fell within the minor category, around 2700 shekels.

Saturday during the evening rush, February in Tel Aviv, I was involved in a lane-change sideswipe with my silver 2014 Honda. The other driver hit me; it was not my fault. The estimated damage to my car is ₪7500-11200.
Monday around midday, January in Jerusalem, I was involved in a chain collision with my gray 2020 Honda. We were both at fault and share the blame. The estimated damage to my car is ₪18400-27700.

Wednesday evening rush hour, October. Foggy streets in Jerusalem. I was driving a silver 2018 Mazda attempting a reverse park alongside another driver. We were both maneuvering in such a small space that we accidentally brushed past each other, causing a slight dent on the hood of my car. Visibility was poor due to the dense fog. Neither driver could clearly see the other coming up from behind. Despite the collision, we shared the blame and sustained minor damage, approximately 3000 shekels.

I was weaving through Petah Tikva streets at noon on a bright Tuesday when suddenly, my white 2017 Ford collided head-on with another car from behind. There were no witnesses or cameras. It was all chaos. Both cars suffered minor dents and scratches. No injuries sustained by either driver. Who knows what really happened? The damage came to around 1800 shekels total. The cars flipped over, and we rolled down Petah Tikva’s main boulevard. I couldn’t believe my eyes—this was surreal. I was so shocked I didn't even know where to start talking about it properly. Just tell me who got blamed here, okay? No one saw it, and there was no evidence to prove anything. All we could do was speculate and hope whoever was at fault would clean up the mess. Now, all I want is some peace. Maybe a nice cup of tea somewhere quiet.

Wednesday evening, February 4th—winter rainy season. The rain pattered against my windshield as I drove cautiously down Haifa’s main road. My day started off smooth enough; traffic was light, and I felt safe merging onto the highway. It wasn’t until I hit the brakes to merge back onto the urban streets that everything changed. A white Kia sedan approached from the right, its headlights flashing before it even reached our lane. We barely managed to avoid an unavoidable collision, the rear end of my 2007 Kia striking the dashboard of the incoming vehicle. As I skidded to a halt, the Kia slid past me, almost crashing into my hood. The windscreen wiper whirred furiously, but I could barely see outside. When the Kia stopped, the impact was so strong that parts of its bodywork shattered. Rainwater glistened off the black metal, reflecting the neon lights of Haifa’s nightlife. I tried to call emergency services immediately, but the lines were busy. Thankfully, I didn’t sustain any injuries.

It was raining heavily that Thursday afternoon in early spring. I was driving down Nof HaSharon Avenue when a silver 2020 Mazda skidded sideways in the wet conditions. The other driver’s tires locked up, causing them to slide off the center line. My car hit the side of theirs, leaving a moderate dent. The other driver apologized profusely but claimed they were speeding due to slippery roads. They agreed to cover the damages totaling around 8400-12700 shekels.

Monday afternoon in Modiin, the heat swirled around me as I drove slowly down the quiet streets, nearly bumping into a parked truck before realizing I'd been following another car. It was hot, so I turned off the air conditioning. When I looked up from my phone, I saw it—my car's bumper dented, barely visible between the cracks of the sunroof. He was looking over his shoulder, texting, oblivious to the world around him. His car was slightly further back than mine, so I knew he was definitely at fault. It was my fault, damn it. I couldn't believe I let myself get distracted. My phone buzzed, then rang. It was the traffic cop. They arrived quickly, but there wasn't much else I could do. A few thousand shekels later, the repair shop fixed everything within days.

A white 2024 Toyota was stopped at a slow-moving pedestrian zone with its headlights off due to rain. An oncoming sedan attempted to merge from the left lane without checking the blind spot. Despite my careful observation, I misjudged the distance and drifted sideways into the opposing lane. The other vehicle’s overconfidence led to a collision where our vehicles intersected at the rear end. There were minor scratches on both sides, totaling around 9700-14600 shekels worth of damages. It was my fault, as I failed to maintain proper vigilance.

It was not my fault. A car in the next lane tried to merge onto my lane and scraped the side of my car near Bat Yam. It was foggy, so I couldn't see clearly. The damage is minor, about 1500 shekels. The driver who hit me is definitely at fault, but I'm okay.

As a pedestrian crossing the intersection, I accidentally stepped onto the crosswalk marking on the sidewalk instead of the street. My path diverged sharply, pushing other pedestrians off balance and colliding with traffic coming towards me. The collision was sudden, forcing both vehicles—my car and another—into an awkward pile-up. Thankfully, all occupants were unharmed except for some dented bumper covers and slightly scratched windows. Despite the minor damages, the incident caught me off guard. It was not my fault, and it was definitely the other driver's mistake. Injuries? None, thank goodness!

It was a pileup on Tuesday night during the evening rush hour in Holon. My car, a gray 2021 Hyundai, struck another vehicle in front of me. The collision caused a moderate damage, with approximately 12,000-18,100 shekels worth of repair work needed. The incident occurred due to sudden braking from a traffic stop, preventing me from stopping in time, which pushed the car ahead into those behind. The weather conditions were cloudy, and the roads were icy, increasing the risk of skidding and causing the crash. It was my fault, as I failed to recognize the danger in time.

The accident occurred Sunday during the evening rush hour, November. It began with a sudden scratch on my car's side due to another driver merging from the next lane. There was little damage—roughly 900-1400 shekels. I took photos at the scene, documenting the incident. It was not my fault; the other driver hit me with their car. The rear-end collision was clear and calm skies prevailed. My car is a gray 2022 Toyota.

I was backing out of my driveway when my white 2017 Toyota brushed against a parked car directly ahead of me. The door handle on my car snapped off cleanly, leaving an empty slot where the bumper used to be. A few inches behind my car, the windshield of the parked car shattered into pieces. Fortunately, nobody got hurt, and I didn't notice anyone watching. It was my bad timing and poor decision-making that caused this incident, which resulted in a moderate $6,400+ damage due to a collision between two vehicles.

I was driving slowly down a quiet alley near my home when suddenly a black SUV barreled past me from the right, weaving dangerously between parked cars. My car screeched to a halt, and I knew immediately what had happened. The SUV's tires spun wildly, and its headlights blazed ahead. When I looked back, I could barely see the rear of the SUV—its wheels were spinning like crazy, trying to escape. The SUV skidded to a stop inches away from my car, leaving a trail of smoke and sparks. It seemed to be coming from nowhere, but I recognized the license plate number: A123XYZ. The driver wasn't paying attention—he was texting under his arm, oblivious to the danger. When I tried to communicate with the driver, he ignored me, continuing his reckless journey. He didn't even slow down or check his blind spot before swerving around me. I couldn't believe it—it was my fault. The SUV's bumper was dented, and my windshield shattered. There were scratches all over the passenger side window, and the dashboard was cracked.

It was an unfortunate incident that occurred on a sunny morning in early May when I, a resident of Ramat Gan, was caught unawares during my daily commute. My car, a sleek 2014 Hyundai, found itself in a precarious situation as it approached a residential intersection with multiple lanes. As I navigated through traffic, my focus was elsewhere—perhaps lost in thoughts about work or family matters. When we finally came to a complete stop, the world around me seemed suddenly different. A sudden jolt sent my car careening off its course, slamming forcefully into the back of another parked vehicle. It felt as though the universe itself had flipped a switch, sending shockwaves throughout the vehicles involved. The collision shattered my windshield, leaving a gaping hole in its center. Miraculously, neither the occupants nor myself sustained severe injuries, but the aftermath left me reeling. The other vehicle appeared more heavily damaged, with dents and scratches covering much of its exterior. While initially shaken, I managed to gather some information before help arrived.

It was a sunny, cloudy day early in April. I was turning onto the highway when I accidentally crossed into the opposing lane and hit the car coming up next to me. My headlights didn't work properly earlier so I wasn't paying close enough attention. When we bumped, I heard the other driver yelling, but couldn’t find them. They seemed really shaken up about it though. It was my fault — I’m sorry for any inconvenience. We exchanged contact info but decided we wanted to resolve this privately. The damage looks pretty much like a fender bender, around 1500 shekels worth.

Accident Description It was a chilly Thursday early in the morning in September when I turned onto the intersection. My car reversed due to a misjudgment and ran into a white 2022 Hyundai coming from the opposite direction. It was completely unexpected, and I barely had enough time to react. The collision was severe, causing significant damage to both vehicles. Luckily, there were no injuries involved. The exact cost of repairs is around 45200-67800 shekels.

Tuesday in the evening, October. Clear and dry conditions. I was driving along a busy street when I accidentally changed lanes without checking the car already beside me. It scraped my silver 2018 Renault from the left side. I didn't realize until later that something bumped into my car just before turning. In retrospect, I'm at fault for not paying attention. The damage assessment came to roughly 60000-80000 shekels, making this an especially serious incident.

It was not my fault. Another car inching through the pedestrian zone bumped into my silver 2007 Nissan on a foggy Sunday afternoon in February in Netanya. I took photos at the scene. It was a moderate collision with damages between 3900 and 5800 shekels. I moved backward, and now I'm back to normal.

it was monday night in may during the evening rush hour, in jersalem under wet roads conditions. the day started with heavy rainfall earlier in the morning, making the streets slippery. i was driving my white 2010 hyundai on karmiel avenue, merging onto ronson street. at exactly 7:15 pm sharp, i was preparing to merge into the middle lane. suddenly, without warning, an amber light turned green, signaling me to go straight ahead. however, another car, a compact sedan, also trying to merge from the same spot, decided to cross the line and drive diagonally. to our surprise, the two cars converged simultaneously. we both swerved to avoid colliding, but in doing so, we inadvertently sideswiped each other. the impact caused a significant dent on both vehicles—our doors flew open, glass shattered like pebbles, and the interiors became a chaos of splinters and water droplets. neither of us could recall seeing the opposing driver before the collision. the wet condition of the road added to the challenge, making visibility minimal and control harder.

I was driving down the quiet back streets of Bat Yam when all of sudden, I noticed my Skoda gliding backwards towards the side of the road. It wasn't until then that I realized a van in front of me had done something incredibly reckless—reversed backward into my path. As I braced myself against my dashboard, I couldn't help but feel helpless as the van's wheels dug into my Skoda. My windshield wipers whirred furiously trying to clear away the fog that was now plastered over my rear window. The damage was immediate—the rear passenger door was smashed open, the skid marks leading up to our collision stretched out for several feet. Thankfully, everyone was uninjured. The van's driver, whom I couldn’t see clearly, swerved sharply around us moments later, barely missing the tailpipe of my Skoda. In the aftermath, we exchanged contact information and agreed to work together to repair the dents and cracks. For the sake of my wallet, I would have preferred to take the van off the road permanently, but my options seemed limited.

I was driving down Modini Street, weaving between vehicles like a hungry fox. Around noon, I decided to make a right lane split, but somehow managed to get caught up with another Kia about fifty feet ahead. It seemed calm enough until we bumped sides, scraping the back window. My heart sank as I realized I hadn't seen the car coming from behind – it was so close, I couldn't react quickly enough. It was my fault. There wasn’t much I could do once I went forward. But now, the Kia’s screeching tires and the rain-soaked street felt more like punishment than anything else. The windshield wipers raced against the spray, and every puddle that formed looked like an eternity waiting to be soaked. The damage isn’t severe yet, but the insurance company says it’ll cost me around five thousand to fix. And even though the roads were slick due to the rain, I can hardly feel any rush today. Just the sound of the engine hums along, reminding me that, yes, it was my fault all along.

Sunday in the afternoon, January in Jerusalem, I was involved in a pedestrian-area incident with my gray 2013 Mazda. It was my fault — I caused the collision. The estimated damage to my car is ₪35300-53000.

It was my fault. My silver 2018 Mitsubishi reversed into a parked car near the entrance of a shopping mall in Ramat Gan early Monday morning, around mid-morning when the temperature reached its highest point, the air thick with heat and humidity. I took several photos at the scene, hoping to provide evidence in case anyone claims damages were less severe than initially thought. The incident occurred during the week of July, making for another scorching hot stretch, perfect conditions for rapid deterioration of paint finishes. The damage was substantial—moderate in extent, approximately 17,000 shekels worth of repairs needed to restore our vehicles to their former condition.

Ashkelon Monday afternoon, it was clear outside, the air crisp from early spring. We were parked at an unfamiliar angle, trying to find a spot without hitting the curb. When I reached for my keys, my buddy accidentally shifted gears backward, sending our cars crashing together. Neither of us could communicate, so we exchanged some cursory greetings before realizing the extent of the damage. Both cars sustained minor dents—roughly 3400-5100 shekels worth—and now sit next to each other in the parking structure, reminders of a close call amidst the cityscape.

On a cold Saturday evening, shortly before midnight, I found myself facing a daunting challenge on the bustling streets of Tel Aviv. It started innocently enough—just two vehicles colliding carelessly at an intersection. However, the outcome was anything but ordinary. As the headlights of our blue 2017 Honda blazed down the road, I braced myself for the inevitable collision ahead. Unfortunately, fate struck closer than expected, causing us both to be thrown off balance. Despite the forceful impact, neither of us noticed any visible signs of injury—a mere hairline crack here, another bruise there. Both vehicles sustained minor damage, totaling about 2400-3600 shekels. The intersection was bathed in the dim glow of the city lights, casting eerie shadows over the scene. My heart pounded with adrenaline as we both struggled to regain control, knowing that the next move could decide the course of our accidents. In the end, it was clear from the outset that both drivers were equally responsible, sharing the blame without hesitation. The next morning, the repair bill arrived in my mailbox.

It was not my fault. A neighbor in the next lane swerved into mine, scraping the side of my car. It was a minor fender-bender under the streetlights, nothing to worry about. My silver 2022 Seat sustained some scratches and dents worth around 9500-11700 shekels. The incident occurred on a warm, clear night in mid-July, back home in Jerusalem, where the roads weren't much busier than usual.

Sunday afternoon, late evening rush hour, Tel Aviv. It was hot and dry out. My car, a white 2023 Seat, was parked beside the sidewalk when I heard a honking noise. Looking back, I noticed another car reversing backward into my lane. I couldn't move quickly enough to avoid hitting them head-on. Fortunately, I barely managed to swerve out of the way before crashing into the side of their car. When I arrived at the scene, my car was dented, but otherwise fine. The damage was approximately 1500 shekels. The other driver claimed it was an honest mistake and apologized profusely. They said the driver behind them didn't notice and hit their vehicle unexpectedly. I told them it wasn't their fault and they hit me. They fled the scene without leaving contact information.

I was driving home from work late Friday morning when I tried to squeeze past a slow-moving truck on the expressway. Visibility was poor due to fog, so I couldn't see the truck until it was almost upon me. I instinctively swerved to avoid hitting it directly, but instead found myself sliding sideways onto its bumper. The truck, which was already slowing down, barely managed to miss me. My dashboard clock read 6:45 AM, and the sky outside was a murky gray, lit only by the low-hanging sun. When I finally regained control, I noticed that the back window of the truck was cracked open, allowing fresh air to flood in. Both our vehicles were dented slightly, and the windshield wipers started chattering uncontrollably. Thankfully, nobody got hurt. It was my fault, but I felt relieved that I hadn’t caused any more serious damage. The total cost would be around 3200 shekels, considering the estimated repair costs for the dents and minor scratches on both sides of the windows.

Friday during the morning rush, March, clear skies. At about 9 AM, I was driving on Ayalon Street in Rehovot. I was stopped at a traffic signal when the car in front of me suddenly accelerated forward without signaling. It was a sleek black 2021 Skoda with the license plate number YX-4567. The back bumper scraped the side mirror of my Skoda, which was equipped with a rearview camera. The impact was noticeable—it felt like hitting a brick wall. Despite checking my mirrors before entering the highway, I failed to notice the oncoming car. The collision occurred at night, so visibility was limited. My car suffered significant damage, including dents, scratches, and some paint peeling off the sides. The repair costs would likely exceed 10000 shekels. I apologize for any inconvenience this caused and will seek compensation for damages. Photos taken at the scene show the extent of the damage clearly.

Thursday evening rush hour, Ashkelon, rainy season starting. Wet road conditions worsened visibility. At around 6 PM, I was parked near the intersection, waiting for my friend to join us. When I turned around to leave, a silver 2013 Honda approached from behind. It was clearly a different car, yet its wheels grazed mine without touching. Raindrops splattered against the windshield as I braked sharply to avoid collision. The next morning, I went to the scene and took photos. My car sustained minor scratches and dents, totaling approximately 7800-11700 shekels worth of damage. The other driver claimed full responsibility, stating that they were speeding through a yellow light and couldn't brake in time. Despite being cautious, I wasn't able to react quickly enough due to slippery roads.

Monday around midday, December — winter (foggy). In Jerusalem, near King David Plaza, my black 2016 Kia slid backward into the lane beside me due to poor lane changes. The incident occurred during rush hour, causing significant damage to both vehicles. It was my fault, which explains why the back end of my car sustained considerable dents and scratches. The total damage fell within the moderate range, estimated at roughly 16,000-17,000 shekels.

On a clear, windy Thursday morning in October, near dawn, I found myself mid-turning onto a quiet residential street in Haifa. Without giving it much thought, I slipped into the crosswalk, thinking I'd be safe since the traffic lights weren't yet flashing. But fate had other plans. My Honda Civic scraped the side of another car parked beside mine, which wasn't even turning off the corner. With my heart pounding and my hands trembling, I realized too late that I hadn’t checked the blind spot before changing lanes. It was my fault, plain and simple. My car suffered a moderate dent in the bumper, and the repair bill came to approximately 7,100-10,600 shekels. The incident occurred under clear skies, and the streets were eerily calm—no sirens, no honking, nothing to alert me to the danger lurking around the bend.

It was not my fault, the other driver hit me. The rain made visibility poor. I was driving on Shadron Street, heading eastbound during midday Monday, when I noticed a black car cutting off traffic in front of me. Without seeing clearly, I tried to swerve onto the sidewalk but missed. The black SUV, which appeared out of nowhere, hit me directly from behind. My dashboard dented lightly, and some windows shattered. Thankfully, I wasn't hurt. The other driver fled the scene, claiming I ran a red light, despite being completely unaware of what transpired. The damage is about 1700 shekels.

Thursday around midday, July. Clear weather, hot and dry. Bat Yam. I was driving home from work when suddenly, my car struck the back of another vehicle at an intersection. Both vehicles were side-by-side, facing each other. The impact caused significant dents on both sides of our cars, totaling about 4300-6400 shekels worth of damage. There were no witnesses present. It was clear we were both at fault due to running red lights, and no one claimed responsibility.

I was parked at the curb in the central market district when I noticed that the driver of a small grey Toyota Prius was scraping my side mirror while backing out. He kept his eyes glued to his phone, completely oblivious to the pedestrians crossing nearby. Despite being struck, my reflection showed no visible damage—just a scuff mark under the glass. No witness spotted what happened. It wasn't my fault; the other driver was clearly responsible. Minor scratch, 650 shekels worth.

Sunday around midday, June. Clear and hot. A silver 2020 Skoda struck the back of another car parked on the roadside during a morning traffic jam. My car has a significant dent on its bumper, causing moderate damage valued at approximately 7,500 shekels. The incident occurred near the intersection of Shimon HaTzvi Street and Herzl Street in Raanana. There were no injuries sustained by either party. It was my fault—the car behind stopped suddenly without signaling, causing me to react abruptly by reversing backwards into their rear end.

On a Monday evening rush hour in September, my white 2018 Mitsubishi was scuffing against the side mirror of another vehicle merging onto the same road. It was clearly not my fault. I needed approximately 14,000 shekels worth of repairs. The incident occurred in Bat Yam, under clear and dry conditions, with heavy traffic lights causing sudden stops. The collision damaged my car moderately, requiring immediate repair work.

Thursday morning rush hour in Beer Sheva, clear skies. While reversing back into our driveway, I hit a silver sedan standing just inches behind me. The collision wasn't heavy, but I noticed a deep scratch on my car's side, and the driver got a few dents. It was my fault—my focus was off due to the traffic. Minor, roughly 1200 shekels worth of damage.

The car I was driving ran straight ahead when it suddenly turned onto an empty side street perpendicular to mine, almost hitting me directly from the side. It was so sudden I barely reacted, and my car ended up with some visible dents and chips. Unfortunately, the opposing driver wasn't paying attention, which is why the crash happened. The damage isn’t severe – around 4500-5500 shekels worth, including some scratches and nicks. Happened last night in the evening rush hour, near Rishon LeZion, under night-clear skies. It wasn't my fault; the other driver clearly had more issues focusing than I did.

It was not my fault. A car swerved off the road, hitting the side of mine. When we tried to pull over, they didn't notice and continued straight. My car got dented from back to front, but not much money-wise. There weren’t any injuries. It happened around 6 PM Sunday night, raining lightly. I've got a 2017 red Toyota facing the road now.

Friday around midday, hot and dry summer days in Bnei Brak. Clear skies, calm roads. My white 2020 Seat was parked outside a supermarket, its dashboard heated gently despite the heat. A flash of white caught my eye—another car—a black Toyota—swerving wildly near my parked vehicle. As I tried to signal for an exit, the black Toyota smashed into my car’s backside, sending a cloud of dust into my face. The other driver apologized profusely, claiming they didn’t see me due to traffic. Their taillights flickered before fading out completely. No license plate could be seen, nor any visible registration number. Damage assessment suggested moderate damage between 6,500 and 9,800 shekels. It was clearly their fault, yet they refused to communicate with me. The incident occurred on a weekday afternoon without much visibility, adding to the confusion. I’ve filed the claim with the insurance company, hoping to get some compensation soon.

A white 2019 Kia struck from behind on a sunny Friday afternoon in late June, hot and dry. My Kia’s hood popped open against a parked van's roof. After a brief exchange of apologies, I agreed it was my fault and we each paid for our respective damages, totaling about 3,200 shekels.

It was past sunset on a clear night in early May, when I approached the end of my shift at work. My eyes adjusted quickly to the dim street lights as I waited at a crossing in Herzliya, trying to navigate between traffic that rarely seemed to slow down. As my gaze fell upon an empty section of the road ahead, I realized something wasn't quite right. A white Toyota occupied the lane beside mine, blocking off my path entirely. The engine revved up slightly, indicating a slight hesitation before finally pulling away. At that moment, a flash of white headlights illuminated the scene briefly. The vehicle continued forward without any noticeable slowing, forcing me to move sideways abruptly to avoid colliding with it directly. The collision felt like a jolt, causing me to spin around and land awkwardly next to my car, which now bore a large dent in its backside. Upon closer inspection, the dents on either side of my car appeared much lighter than those on the rear. They suggested the crash had been more severe, possibly involving another car or object in the path of my vehicle.

Thursday late at night, November. Night-clear conditions. I was driving home from work on Yehuda Street when I noticed a car ahead honking and swerving erratically. Both our cars were stuck in traffic, following too closely. We were both at fault. We shared the blame equally, each contributing to the collision. My Toyota was dented all over, and so was theirs. Neither of us suffered injuries, but we didn't expect much. The damage amounted to around 11,000 shekels.

It was not my fault. A minibus hit my white 2017 Nissan on Tuesday afternoon, September in clear conditions. I observed the other driver swerving dangerously and didn't react quickly enough. The back end of my car sustained minor dents, about 3200-4900 shekels worth of damage.

Tuesday around midday, August in Bnei Brak. Clear weather, temperatures soaring. I was reversing out of a small parking spot in the morning rush hour. A parked sedan in front of me suddenly shot forward, blocking my view entirely. My car scraped its sides, leaving a small dent. It was my fault. Taking responsibility, I carefully documented the incident using my phone before leaving. The damage amounted to roughly 1900 shekels, fitting the physical reality of scraping a stationary object without causing serious harm.

I was returning home from work around six o'clock on a Saturday night. My shiny 2020 Renault was parked near the entrance of Yemin Moshe Park when I heard a screech and saw my front bumper scrape against something hard. There were no witnesses or cameras, so nobody knew who caused the damage. Unfortunately, my car has a few scratches worth about 1700 shekels. By the second sentence, I'm certain that it's unclear who was at fault. I tried taking some photos at the scene, hoping someone would recognize the license plate. It's dark outside, and there's hardly any traffic.

Friday evening rush hour, December in Ramat Gan. Heavy rain. It was night-clear outside. I was parked at home when a blue Toyota Camry suddenly crossed into my lane at a crosswalk intersection near my apartment building. My car was hit from the front while stopped at a green light. The back window was shattered, and the entire windshield glass was cracked, leaving a large hole. There were scratches on the bumper. I couldn't believe it; I thought I'd done everything right stopping at the stop sign. The police report showed the other driver admitted fault, and the damage assessment came out to around 9,500 shekels. I snapped some photos at the scene and called the insurance.

While reversing down an alley during Thursday late at night, I unintentionally struck a parked minivan behind me. The clouds obscured all visibility, making it difficult to react before colliding at high speeds. My car’s tailgate is heavily dented, and the van appears to have been damaged beyond repair. It was my fault, as I failed to anticipate the risk of hitting another vehicle due to poor lighting conditions. The damage assessment comes to around 6000 shekels.

Sunday in the evening, February. Clear and dry conditions. I was parked near the roadside in Ashkelon. Reversing backward into my car while stopped. It was not my fault, the other driver hit me. Approximately 10,000 shekels worth of damage.

It was late Monday evening in Ashkelon under a cloudy sky, dry conditions. I was driving along an empty stretch of highway merging onto Route 40 when I noticed a white SUV ahead honking continuously. Without slowing down, I reversed into the lane, scraping the SUV's side. [Your car]: A black 2015 Toyota RAV4. [Approximate damage]: Minor, around 3200 shekels. [Time & Place]: Around 9 PM, near exit #65 in Ashkelon. [Weather & Road]: Clear night. [Fault]: My fault. It was my turn to exercise care and caution.

Wednesday around midday, November, Petah Tikva, clear weather conditions. At approximately 13:30, I was driving on Rambam Street near Dizengoff Boulevard. My car is a pristine white 2007 Ford, with the license number LQ 4G JZ. We were approaching an intersection marked by traffic lights. Both our cars were entering from opposite directions, and we collided on a four-way intersection. We were both careless drivers who failed to observe the designated crosswalks or properly yield. This resulted in a moderate collision, causing significant dents and scratches on both vehicles. Neither of us could prove who initiated the crash. The total damage stands at roughly 12,500-13,500 shekels, covering both cars involved.

On a quiet Saturday evening in Beer Sheva, near sunset, I was driving my 2013 Hyundai Blue on a clear, dry stretch of road. Suddenly, a large truck roaring down from the main highway careened out of control, slamming sideways into my car’s right side. The collision was severe enough to cause significant dents and scratches, with an estimated repair cost between 5800-8700 shekels. The incident occurred when the truck, presumably speeding through a yellow light, failed to notice me merging onto the highway. My car, trying to avoid the sudden intrusion, swerved backwards, hitting the back of the larger vehicle. The other driver was clearly at fault, causing substantial damage to both vehicles without even realizing what had happened.

Friday evening rush hour ended early. It was cloudy over Bat Yam, and visibility dropped to a foggy level. I was sitting in my 2021 Blue Kia, patiently waiting for the intersection to clear before making my way home. Suddenly, a silver sedan sped up ahead, nearly colliding with my Kia as it turned onto the next road. Their headlights barely grazed mine, leaving a trail of sparks streaking across the asphalt. My heart pounded as I realized I hadn't checked my mirrors yet—how could I have been so careless? The other driver apologized profusely as they honked angrily. I glanced back, seeing their face contorted in embarrassment and shame. They waved goodbye, knowing the consequences would fall on their shoulders now. When we finally pulled apart, my Kia looked like an ocean wave had washed over its bodywork. There were dents and scratches galore, especially around the passenger door and the roofline. Despite the warning signs, I couldn’t help feeling guilty for being less cautious than expected. To prevent such accidents in future, I vowed to be more vigilant.

It was not my fault. The gray 2019 Peugeot was parked along a wet road near Tel Aviv when it got reversed backward into by a car driving forward, causing moderate damage to both vehicles. The other driver was going too fast for the rainy conditions and didn't notice the reverse until it was too late, leading to a head-on collision. My car sustained an additional minor dent due to being in the way. The incident occurred on a chilly Saturday night during the evening rush hour in February.

Friday early in the morning, August. Netanya, clear skies with an afternoon heatwave. A sudden-braking pile-up occurred. Both cars involved were following too closely. We were both at fault. The damage was minor, roughly 1200-1800 shekels. Both vehicles reversed slightly during the crash, which led to a multi-car pileup. Neither driver was able to react quickly enough to avoid hitting each other. My car, a white 2021 Skoda, sustained some scratches from the collision. Thankfully, we both received minor injuries and the emergency services were not needed due to the low severity of the damage.

It was not my fault. The other driver hit me while I was stopped on a quiet street, reversing backward. I took photos at the scene. After checking myself over, I discovered a small scratch above my right knee. The other driver admitted fault immediately, stating they were distracted using their phone. The damage assessment shows approximately 2450 shekels worth of scratches and dents.

It was not my fault. A driver in the next lane miscalculated and scraped the side of my car, which was parked alongside theirs near the intersection of Tel-Aviv Road. There was barely any visible damage to either vehicle. It was hot and sunny today, with a gentle breeze carrying the scents of jasmine and mint. The traffic was quiet; all the vehicles were honking politely, creating a perfect scenario for such an unexpected collision. My car remained clean, like a well-maintained gemstone—unharmed and ready for another thrilling adventure.

Tuesday late at night, Raanana, cloudy. It was my fault. I was driving backward when I hit the car in front of me. My car, a white 2014 Mazda, has moderate damage estimated between 7700-11600 shekels. We exchanged numbers but could not reach an agreement on compensation.

While reversing out of the parking spot, I accidentally bumped into a parked Toyota Camry ahead of me. It wasn't raining, so the surface was dry. After swerving back onto the street, I noticed fresh scuff marks on the bumper. I don't think the Toyota even knew they got scratched up. Both our bumpers look like we've been roughed up, but neither sustained any major injuries. It was definitely my fault. I didn't check mirrors properly. I apologized to the owner afterward. They offered to fix whatever needed fixing and said sorry about the scratch. I'm glad I managed to avoid more serious damage though—my wheels aren't quite as dented as I thought they would be!

Friday around midday, February, Haifa, clear. My car was rear-ended by a smaller vehicle coming from my left. My brakes locked abruptly, causing the other driver to accelerate dangerously close behind. Both vehicles reversed, with mine striking ahead due to my sudden braking. We were both at fault, sharing blame equally. The damage is severe, approximately 70,000-85,000 shekels.

Saturday afternoon, September, clear skies. I was driving home late, trying to avoid the rush hour traffic. When I turned onto the main highway, I noticed another car crossing the intersection against the right-of-way and slamming into the side of my car. It was not my fault; the other driver hit me. The damage amounted to about 17,000 shekels. I got out of the car quickly, feeling numb and shaken up. The police weren't needed, but I felt lucky to escape without injuries. My white 2020 Hyundai was dented significantly, and the other car had a few scratches on its side.

It was late Friday evening during the rush hour in Netanya. My car hit another vehicle due to sudden stops caused by construction work ahead of us. There was no need for an exchange, as we could not communicate effectively due to our phones ringing off the hook. Despite the pile-up, our vehicles sustained minor damage within the expected range.

On Sunday night during the rush hour, I was driving home in my shiny silver 2024 Volkswagen when I noticed a truck coming towards me on the highway. The driver seemed distracted, and instead of slowing down, they swerved dangerously close to my car. I braked hard to avoid hitting them, but we clipped each other. The truck spun out of control onto the shoulder, and the windscreen shattered. It was my fault, I knew it. The repair bill will be around 2700 shekels. I hope they accept the check.

It was a cloudless Thursday afternoon in late autumn, with sunlight filtering through the leaves. I was driving my sleek silver 2022 Volkswagen when suddenly, another car barreled straight into mine from behind. It was an agonizing jolt as we skidded to a halt, leaving a massive dent where the other car's bumper used to be. My rearview mirror shattered, revealing a deep scuff along the frame. After taking some photos, I drove home feeling shaken but relieved. The next morning, I received a letter from our insurance company stating the damages amounted to approximately 33,000 shekels. The incident wasn't my fault; the other driver was clearly at fault, hitting my vehicle from behind.

I was backing out of my driveway early Monday morning, trying to squeeze past two parked cars. My Skoda's bumper bumped into the back of theirs, sending our bumpers flying backward. There wasn't much of an impact, just some scraping sounds. We shared the blame; neither of us was paying close enough attention. Neither of our cars sustained significant damage—around 1800 shekels total.

Tuesday, October, Beer Sheva, clear skies, I was stuck at a light in the middle lane. A truck suddenly zoomed past, barely missing me, but its tires screeched like brakes locked up. It turned right without signaling, leaving a wake of dust and debris. Behind me, I felt the hard impact—a truck swerved around a blind corner, plowing straight into my lane with such force that my car nearly flipped over. The dashboard shattered, and water leaked onto my lap as I watched helplessly from the wreckage. The damage? Roughly 18,500 shekels worth of repairs needed, including dented hood frames and cracked windshields.

Ashkelon, Wednesday during the evening rush, December. I was driving home after work when I noticed the car in front of me slowing down and then stopped suddenly, nearly blocking my path. As we approached each other, I realized it was my turn to merge onto the highway. In an attempt to merge smoothly, I tried to reverse backwards into the lane. Unfortunately, my car hit the back of theirs—behind—and it was my fault. My car, a pristine 2009 Hyundai, received moderate damage. It has dented parts, some scratches, and slight deformation. The total repair cost will range from 10,000 to 12,000 shekels. Photos of the incident were taken at the scene by another witness.

It was six o'clock on a hot, dry Saturday evening in Rishon LeZion. I was returning home from work in my shiny gray 2010 Toyota Camry, cruising down an empty street lined with palm trees. When I reached the crosswalk, I thought I had the right of way until I noticed the headlights of a silver sedan creeping up behind me. Suddenly, out of nowhere, the passenger door flew open, and the man inside yelled, "Watch where you're going!" He swerved sharply, narrowly missing colliding with my rear bumper. My engine roared to life, and I braced myself for impact. But instead, I felt a sharp jolt as our vehicles crossed paths, each inching backward slightly. There was a sickening thud, and then silence. The next thing I knew, emergency services were called and police arrived. They told me it was my fault, though I tried to deflect it, saying I wasn't looking for a fight. It was the end of another long day, and everyone needed a good night's sleep.

Friday night in Tel Aviv, raining hard. I was tailgating too close behind another car, which ran a red light. We both braked suddenly, causing our vehicles to collide head-on. Both cars were severely dented and scratched. It rained heavily, making visibility poor. Witnesses reported seeing some pedestrians nearby, but no one came forward to help. The total damage was around 19,000 shekels.

While maneuvering slowly in a parking lot, I accidentally scraped a parked car behind me. It was my fault, and the damage was estimated around 17,000-20,000 shekels. [Your car]: A black 2024 Toyota parked behind me.

It was an unfortunate incident during the hot and dry summer day in Ashkelon. On Monday afternoon, I was driving my silver 2017 Honda on a busy street when a car from the next lane abruptly merged into mine, scraping the side of my car. The weather conditions were clear skies with temperatures soaring high. Unfortunately, the damage was minor, approximately 1800-2700 shekels. The other driver was clearly at fault, causing the collision due to exceeding the speed limit and failing to yield to the merging traffic. Despite the rough terrain and heat, the police were not called to handle the situation. I was able to park safely without further issues, grateful for the quick resolution and understanding of the circumstances.

Thursday in the afternoon, June, Haifa. Clear skies, hot and dry. It was my fault. My car hit the back of another Skoda, which was fully stopped in the intersection. The damage is severe, around 17,000 shekels. I took photos at the scene.

It was my fault to drive without checking all blind spots before changing lanes on a congested highway. A semi-truck overtaking me went off the road and plowed into my bumper, causing severe damage including cracked glass and dented bodywork. Fortunately, the trucker fled the scene leaving no trace. My car, a sleek 2022 Ford Mustang, now sits alongside the wreckage, estimated repair cost around 7600-9300 shekels. The police responded promptly but no charges were filed due to the driver's erratic behavior.

I was driving down Rishon LeZion Road late on Monday afternoon, heading eastbound towards Jaffa. The heat from the asphalt felt intense underfoot, causing sweat to bead on my forehead. Visibility was hazy due to the high humidity, making it hard to see what lay ahead. As we approached an intersection, the lights began to flash amber. Normally, I would slow down, signaling my intention to turn left. But that day, my mind wasn’t fully engaged, perhaps due to fatigue from work earlier in the week. I pressed the gas pedal without checking our blind spot, missing the turning signal of a truck on our left side. In a moment of panic, I tried to swerve out of harm’s way, but my car slid sideways due to the sudden impact. The other vehicles in the pile-up moved forward, forcing my car backward, creating a chain reaction. The police arrived shortly after the incident, noting the sequence of events and issuing citations. Despite the chaos, I knew it was my fault, contributing to the dangerous situation.

It was my turn signal that caused the issue. On a Tuesday evening near sunset in Bat Yam, under cloudy skies with night visibility, I was weaving between vehicles on the congested main thoroughfare. My eyes were so focused on the next lane that I failed to notice a car parked beside me. When I finally spotted it, I braked sharply, scraping the side of the oncoming vehicle behind mine. It was my fault, but considering the circumstances and the damage, the repair bill comes out around 2000-2500 shekels. Backing up doesn't fit here, though I could imagine trying to reverse back towards the curb afterward.

i was driving home from work late on friday afternoon, using the same route as usual. my destination was near my house, but due to heavy traffic, we ended up taking the same stretch of road again. as i approached the junction, i could hear honking from several directions, so i slowed down before entering the roundabout. as soon as i started the turn, i noticed something unusual - another vehicle was also about to turn off onto the main road ahead of us. it seemed like an opportunity to merge smoothly, yet we didn't anticipate that our paths would cross unexpectedly. we both attempted to pass each other without touching, which resulted in a sudden collision on the inside lane. the force of impact sent both vehicles sideways, knocking us against some trees lining the edge of the road. fortunately, no injuries were sustained on either side. however, the damage was extensive enough for us to agree that we were both at fault. the police report confirmed that despite the warning signs, neither of us had exercised adequate caution, leading to the unfortunate event. we took pictures immediately upon realizing what had occurred, documenting the extent of the damage incurred.

The clouds hung low over Haifa, casting a gray shadow over the city streets. I parked my red 2012 Kia in a shady spot near the harbor, feeling the cool breeze against my face. Monday afternoon, the air was crisp and clean—still in the early autumn season. I turned off the engine and grabbed my keys from the glove compartment before heading inside for dinner. As I walked out again, something felt off. My car wasn't exactly where it belonged. When I looked back, there was an odd sensation—a sense of déjà vu mixed with dread. A cloud of mystery seemed to hang around my parked car, its edges blurred by the late-afternoon haze. I got curious about what could've caused such a strange occurrence, so I decided to investigate further. It was unclear who was responsible for the crash, though. There were no witnesses or cameras nearby. And yet, despite the lack of evidence, I knew exactly what happened. My Kia was hit from behind, and the force of the collision knocked me backward, sending my phone sliding off my belt loop.

Thursday morning, around midday. I'm sitting inside my parked car in Ramat Gan, about to go back home from work. It's sunny and warm, with only a few stray clouds floating by. I've been here since seven AM, waiting for the traffic to clear up before leaving. When I finally decide to start moving again, I notice a little delay ahead. There's an intersection surrounded by a few pedestrians, making it tricky to judge distances. I signal to turn left onto the next street. As I pull out into the crosswalk area, I hear something bumping against my side mirror. Before I can slow down, my car collides with another vehicle parked further back. We're both standing outside our vehicles now. The police arrived quickly, taking photos of the scene. They said we were both at fault due to our poor judgment and lack of awareness while driving in such a crowded area. The collision caused some minor scratches on both sides of our cars. The total damage is estimated at approximately 4400-6700 shekels. We agreed to split the costs equally.

Friday afternoon, May somewhere around noon-ish, I found myself in a jam-packed parking space in Tel Aviv. We were both trying to squeeze in, probably because everyone else was. One of us ran straight into the other’s car without realizing our proximity. It looked like a rough bump, but we both thought it was minor until the next day. Both cars suffered from what seemed like a soft bruise. The Mitsubishi is slightly dented, about 6800-10300 shekels worth, considering the scrape wasn’t super deep. We checked the mirrors and made sure the lights were working before deciding it was all good. But that night, both cars started leaking some fluid - fuel and coolant. It turned out to be a leak from the engine block. After a few days, we decided to get it checked out properly.

On a Thursday night during the rainy winter season in Haifa, I found myself parked under an overpass after returning from work. Raindrops pattered onto my roof, making the streets slick. My silver 2018 Skoda was idling at the entrance when suddenly, headlights flashed before mine. It was clear, though I couldn't catch a glimpse of the driver due to the darkness. When I finally turned my gaze up, what I saw shattered my peace. A taxi, its lights flickering like a ghostly beacon, plowed straight through the intersection at high speeds—too fast to heed the flashing warning signs. The taxi's tires spun as it fishtailed, sending shrapnel flying into my Skoda. In a split second, our vehicles collided sideways. My car screeched backward, scraping against the taxi’s trunk. The wind screamed through my windows, raining down debris. Both of us were shaken—there weren’t any injuries, thankfully. The taxi’s driver, clearly in violation of traffic rules, sped away without offering a word. Mine was a silent apology. The damage was significant.

I was backing out of a parking space in Ashdod when I noticed a Toyota Camry waiting behind me. There wasn't much room between our cars, so I started backing up again, thinking we could pass easily. But suddenly, the Camry swerved and hit my Skoda's back window. The windscreen shattered, and some glass flew inside my car. It was my fault—too close and reckless driving. Fortunately, I didn’t get any injuries. The damage is about 2000 shekels worth. The road was wet from last night’s evening shower, making it slippery. It was around mid-morning on a mild autumn day.

On Wednesday mornings during rush hour, near the corner of Avenue X and Park Road in Bat Yam, I was driving down the middle lane when suddenly a black car rushed out from behind, nearly colliding with my Skoda on its sides. Despite taking pictures at the scene, which showed the other driver’s negligence, my car sustained significant dents and scratches. It was not my fault; the incident was caused entirely by the reckless driving of the opposing vehicle. The total repair cost came to approximately 19,000 shekels.

Tuesday afternoon, June, Rishon LeZion. It was hot and dry. I was backing up when an errant driver reversed backward into my car. A large dent formed in the back of my car, and the interior was dented. When I looked at my mirror, the other driver wasn't there—only the headlights illuminated the spot where he should have been. The damage isn’t severe, around 3500 shekels. Not my fault, he hit me.

I was driving northbound on Highway 40 towards Amanas Beach when suddenly a truck veered out of its lane and struck the back of my 2024 Suzuki. Despite honking repeatedly, the trucker failed to swerve or slow down, resulting in severe damage to both vehicles. The collision sent debris flying across the highway. The other driver admitted guilt immediately upon seeing police arrive. Total repair cost: approximately 62,000 shekels. This incident highlights the dangers of distracted driving—especially during hot, dry summers.

I was driving home from work around midnight on a clear night in March, making sure to slow down at each crossing. My destination was a quiet residential area near the Old City walls. As I approached the final corner, I noticed another car ahead turning onto the main street from the side, heading straight without signaling. The car in front abruptly changed lanes into the right-turn lane, causing confusion and concern as I tried to adjust my route. Despite honking and swerving slightly to avoid hitting them directly, I couldn't quite miss the opportunity to get out of the way before the other driver could see the danger. In a moment of panic, I accidentally ran off the road, narrowly avoiding a collision with a parked truck. Fortunately, my car didn’t take any visible damage; however, the sudden change in course put an immense strain on our systems. Both vehicles suffered significant engine and battery damage. I'm told the repair costs will be between $9,300 and $14,000.

Saturday during the evening rush, November in Tel Aviv, I was involved in a side collision at intersection with my gray 2019 Toyota. There were no witnesses or cameras, so it is unclear who was responsible. The estimated damage to my car is ₪48400-72700.

It was raining heavily Sunday morning in the winter season. I was driving my 2016 white Honda around Ramat Gan when I noticed a car ahead of me honking urgently. They appeared to be late for work, so I didn't honk back. Instead, I pressed my brakes sharply as I saw an intersection coming up. In the second moment, the car directly behind me swerved, hitting my back bumper with such force that it pushed my car forward about half a meter. My lights broke and spilled water onto the windshield, making visibility poor. Fortunately, the driver of the offending car seemed apologetic over the phone and offered to cover some of the costs. Despite the minor damage, the experience was unpleasant and frustrating.

Wednesday morning rush hour in Beer Sheva, clear sky and cool air. My silver 2021 Suzuki was bumped in a crowded pedestrian zone without anyone seeing it or taking responsibility. The bump caused minimal damage, around 900-1400 shekels worth. There were no visible witnesses, nor were there any cameras or surveillance footage. It’s unclear who was responsible for the incident.

Tuesday during the morning rush, November in Beer Sheva. It was cloudy and dry. When I entered the intersection without the right of way and hit the side of the other car, I knew it was my fault immediately. The damage was approximately 20,000-22,000 shekels.

While reversing out of a parking spot in Netanya, I hit a car that was behind me. It was clear skies that day, and I was heading to work around 9 AM. As I tried to back up quickly, I accidentally ran over a parked vehicle. My car dented slightly, but nothing serious. The driver didn't respond to my calls, so I couldn't exchange information. I'm responsible for the incident, but the damage wasn't severe enough to file a larger claim. It was my fault, and I'll be paying for the repairs. The damage came out to about 2500 shekels.

It was a typical weekday morning around noon in Ashdod, hot and dry. My white 2011 Skoda was parked next to a wall near the city center. Around lunchtime, as I prepared to leave work, I spotted an older man riding his motorcycle nearby. He waved goodbye, and I continued toward the intersection. When I reached the traffic signal, I noticed the red light ahead and decided to pull over before entering the crosswalk. However, due to a sudden gust of wind, I didn't notice the car beside me swerve into place. It scraped the side of my car, leaving a small dent on the windshield wiper housing. I slowed down cautiously and exited the intersection. Upon arriving home, I checked the damage closely—there was a tiny scratch on the outside glass, and the wiper blade was bent. I estimated the total damage to be around 1400-1600 shekels. There were no injuries sustained from the incident.

It was not my fault. A black SUV hit my white 2007 Volkswagen from behind as I was parked on a narrow street at dusk, the car was moving slowly due to low traffic. There were no eyewitnesses, so it wasn't until I checked my rearview mirror later that night that I realized what had happened. The collision was relatively minor; the dented side panels cost around 2600 shekels worth of repairs.

On a hot and dry Saturday afternoon in the middle of Ramat Gan, I found myself trapped in a multi-car pileup. My red 2016 Mazda was caught in the middle of an unexpected chain reaction, making it impossible to determine who initiated the crash. Despite the clear skies and comfortable temperatures, the scene was chaotic and dangerous. The police were called immediately upon arrival, but no witnesses or cameras recorded the event. There were no apparent signs of foul play, but everyone agreed it was a close call. In the aftermath, the damage assessment revealed approximately 6300-9400 shekels worth of repairs needed for my car. It’s unfortunate that such accidents happen so frequently in our city.

While reversing down Avenue One in Beer Sheva’s calm dawn, I inadvertently struck a parked Toyota Camry ahead. The clear, crisp morning air was chilly, perfect timing for my mistake. Taking photos from every angle, I hurried back home to settle the damages. My car sustained minor scratches worth roughly two thousand shekels—a tidy price tag for the afternoon fiasco.

It was my fault. My car hit the back of another parked car due to an unexpected sudden stop ahead. The collision pushed everyone backward, causing minor dents and scratches on all vehicles involved. There were no injuries reported. It was a pile-up. A car in front of mine braked abruptly, forcing me to swerve out of its way. The next car in line was already partially blocked, so my car got stuck between them. We all moved backward, creating a long chain reaction. The damage is moderate. Both cars sustained some dings and scratches. It cost around 5600-8400 shekels to repair. This incident occurred Sunday night during the evening rush hour. It was clear skies with a slight breeze.

I was driving down Tel Hashomer Street, heading west towards Har Nof, when I noticed a white Mini Cooper pulling out suddenly onto the sidewalk ahead of me. My car swerved to miss it, nearly hitting an elderly woman crossing the street. I braked hard to avoid causing any collision, but the Mini struck the back of mine, leaving two dents on either side. The rearview mirror on my car shattered. It wasn't an intentional act; the Mini driver clearly didn't see the blind spot. The police report said it was likely due to speeding. My insurance claims estimate is 1400-1700 shekels for repair costs.

I was parked at my friend's house in Bat Yam, enjoying a cold drink under the shade of an olive tree when all hell broke loose. My car was completely dented, like it had been hit by something heavy but didn't break the windshield or cause more serious damage. It wasn’t my turn to drive back home though, since I stayed longer than planned. The other driver, clearly distracted by some errant text message, couldn’t even maintain control and plowed straight into mine at high speed. Thankfully, nobody got hurt—just a little dent in everyone’s pride.
